picks.title: AlphaGenome 2: Deciphering how cells read DNA to better understand disease
picks.rationale: Primary-source release of a next-gen DNA sequence model that predicts variant effects per human cell type/state; major new model, not previously covered.
picks.excerpt: DeepMind's next-generation DNA sequence model bridges single-cell biology and human genetics, predicting how genetic variants affect specific human cell types and cell states to help interpret disease risk.

picks.title: AI-designed metasurface could make cameras far more light-efficient
picks.rationale: Neural-network inverse design yields a nanoscale colour router that beats absorptive filters; concrete physics result with a clear imaging payoff.
picks.excerpt: A neural-network-assisted inverse-design search produced a nanoscale colour router that delivers substantially more light to an image sensor than conventional absorptive colour filters.

picks.title: OpenAI's 'shepherds' affirm blockbuster physics result
picks.rationale: Follow-up with a new concrete event: a David Gross-led committee affirmed the AI-generated Yang-Mills existence proof and released an explanation plus Lean formal verification on Nov 10.
picks.excerpt: A committee led by Nobel laureate David Gross affirmed OpenAI's AI-generated proof of the existence of quantum Yang-Mills theory and released an explanation plus Lean formal verification on Nov 10, while noting they do not yet fully understand the proof; the mass-gap question remains open.

picks.title: Machine learning reveals how often fish schooling evolved—and repeatedly disappeared
picks.rationale: PNAS study using a text transformer plus computer vision across 2,839 species to show schooling evolved ~60 times and was lost ~320 times; AI as an evolutionary-biology method.
picks.excerpt: Cornell researchers used a text transformer on species descriptions plus computer vision and 3D reconstruction of fish photos/videos to classify 2,839 species, finding schooling evolved independently ~60 times and was lost ~320 times over 350 million years (PNAS).

picks.title: People project a specific racial identity onto artificial intelligence, study finds
picks.rationale: Five-study, three-country JPSP paper showing people code AI as White, which shifts persuasiveness and task allocation; fresh psychology finding about AI perception.
picks.excerpt: Across five studies (~2,400 participants in the U.S., India and Japan), people associated AI with Whiteness even without human features, which modestly raised AI's persuasiveness; AI described as trained on Black and Latino adults was assigned less demanding work (Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, Purdue/Northwestern).
